title: What If Columbus's Crew Had Turned Back?
topic: What if Columbus's crew had turned back? (October 1492)
mechanism: Columbus kept a shorter distance count for his crew (as Las Casas's summary of his log tells it); after the 10 October complaint and, some later writers say, a three-day deal, floating clues and a 2 a.m. sighting kept the ships going, and the crossing started the Columbian exchange, which someone else would almost certainly have started soon anyway.

beats.hook: Columbus lied to his own crew about distance, and it almost wasn't enough: one continuous push past the lantern onto Columbus writing in two logbooks at once in his cabin.
beats.but: Three small ships sail west from the Canaries into an empty ocean: the voyage is longer than anyone aboard has known.
beats.then: He keeps two counts of distance, a true one and a shorter one for the crew (two labelled logbooks).
beats.conflict: Weeks pass, no land; on October tenth the crew has had enough: 'Admiral, turn back!'
beats.pivot: You see, Columbus keeps two counts of distance: the TRUE log is slammed under the FOR THE CREW log as a sailor bursts in (the pivot comes early here: the approved script states the trick first).
beats.so: Clues in the water, a 2 a.m. cry of 'Land!'; what if they had turned back? Portugal reached Brazil in 1500 anyway; but this crossing started the great swap, potatoes and chocolate east, smallpox west.
beats.closing: A lie, one tense night, a few twigs; and Columbus claimed the lookout's reward, saying he had seen a light first.

seed.what: The two logbooks on Columbus's desk (TRUE / FOR THE CREW), and Columbus himself in period dress

CabinSet at night, cold blue moonlight through the stern windows, one candle
DeckSet (new): the Santa María's waist, mast, rail, barrels; noon light drifting to orange dusk
Room: a friar's study, red-brown panelling, two writing desks (the summary, the later writer)

SeaSet + rigging: the Pinta's crow's nest at 2 a.m. under the moon, a pale cliff on the horizon

Room: a long trading table spanning EAST and WEST, crates POTATOES / CACAO / SMALLPOX, lanterns on the west end
SeaSet at dawn: the three ships before the island, rose-pink sky

characters.look: Columbus: long grey-white hair, dark red doublet with a black vest and a wide black hat (period costume, no cap)
A bearded sailor in a faded blue smock and a red kerchief
A young sailor in an ochre smock with a brown vest
Rodrigo de Triana (the lookout): young, dark hair, white shirt, green kerchief
Las Casas: a Dominican friar in a white habit with a black cloak
A later chronicler (Oviedo, unnamed on screen) in a dark green doublet and a hat
Indigenous villagers on the west end of the swap table, shown plainly and respectfully, no caricature

gags.what: A sailor bursts into the cabin and Columbus slams the TRUE logbook shut and shoves it under the other one
A sailor leans out over the rail to scoop the berry branch and nearly topples over; his mate grabs his belt
The lookout holds out his hand for the 10,000 MARAVEDIS purse; Columbus points at the sky ('a light!') and pockets it

format_note: The ships are drawn at cartoon scale; the carved stick and the berry branch are drawn about twice their real size so they read on a phone. Columbus's looks are illustrative. The logbooks show words only, no league numbers.
